script.text: Mother put Szeth to work, which he realized was what he’d wanted in wandering this direction. He busied himself mashing vegetables with vigor. No chopping—the Farmer owned several fine steel knives, crafted by an Honorbearer using their Soulcasting art, but none were available. So he used a clay mortar and pestle to crush the onions, garlic, and spices together—each of which had been lightly braised to soften them.

script.text: It was good active work. In the distant darkness, music started playing as someone got out their flute. This cut off shortly, leaving the nervous bleating. The Farmer wouldn’t want music to give away their position, in case raiders slipped past his soldiers. That was why they had no bonfires, and minimal lanterns. Indeed, Szeth worked at his mashing only by the shadowy light of the firepit and the oven.

script.text: Szeth enjoyed working on meals like this, even if the onions made his eyes water. The Cook—who oversaw the feeding of the people and made certain nobody ever went hungry—had created interesting wooden ladles for measuring. The one Szeth used had the bowl of the ladle split into three sections, with some smaller measuring sections along the handle. All he had to do was fill the largest compartment with oil, the middle one with onion, and the next with garlic. Then he filled the three little divots on the handle with salt, ground chili pepper, and coriander, respectively. He could dump that all into his pestle and begin mashing, and would always have the correct proportions.
script.speaker: Narrator

script.text: Once that was done, he added it to the clay cooking dish—with one scoop of lentils and two of water. The measuring ladle let him work without supervision, and he enjoyed it specifically because it was impossible to do it wrong. Why couldn’t more things in life have a tool like this for exact measuring?

The girthy woman was dressed all in color, with a red skirt, blue sash, and yellow blouse. script.text: It was relatively easy to get men riled up and energized if there was only one decisive battle to win. This extended—but aggressive—siege was different. Small numbers of defenders meant frequent rotations into the dome. It meant holding back an enemy, instead of conquering plateaus or taking ground. But perhaps re-forming the truth into what you wanted it to be was not a trait merely of liars, but of all human beings.

His spren had stopped talking to him except to issue stiff commands. Nightblood spent his days chatting with the Honorblades. Kaladin and Nale argued. Did they care about Szeth, or merely about proving one another wrong? Dared he think such thoughts about a holy being such as Nin-son-God?

script.text: Szeth glanced over his shoulder at the two men. Blue uniform and black. The man who had left him to die, and the man who had saved him. The man who claimed to care for Szeth, and the one who only cared about the law. A piece of him was angry at them both for pulling him between them.

script.text: The thick, wet air reminded her of the first whiff of a cup of tea, fat with steam and the smell of herbs. script.text: Each idea led to answers that felt wrong. Emotional Core Theory taught her to look toward what drove participants: What emotions might be causing them to act as they did? Was there an intangible, emotional reason that Odium wanted this city? Perhaps failing to take it a year ago still rankled, and so he’d come for vengeance.

script.text: Yet this was a new Odium—and while the power might want vengeance, who knew what the new Vessel wanted? She was on shaky ground to assume she could reason their motives. Plus, she’d never liked assuming that her opponents were making mistakes. Yes, it was important to recognize and exploit missteps, but underestimating foes was a bad habit that led to worse surprises. If you instead assumed your enemies were making the

script.text: Hiking through the chasms reawakened Venli’s childhood, and she loved it. Even with the red lightning above and the terrible way thunder echoed down here. Even with the otherwise absolute darkness broken only by their frail gemstones. Even with a flow of water that came up to her knees at times. Even with the stench of death and the ancient corpses they sometimes passed.

script.text: She loved the sounds of trickling water, of vines constricting, of cremlings on the walls—and the steady, dangerous splashing of the chasmfiends behind. She would periodically glance back and see them there—wedged between the walls, using their many legs to maneuver, their faces like chunks of broken rock. She’d panic briefly, then attune Awe. These were their allies now.
script.speaker: Narrator

script.text: She closed her eyes, listening to that strange tone she followed, growing more firm and pure as they traveled inward. She breathed in the potent air, walked through the darkness with her hands out to the sides.

script.text: The water flow, although shallow, was growing treacherous. The chasms had a mostly flat floor, the result of crem settlement competing against erosion and creating a kind of equilibrium that prevented the chasms from filling in. She thought the erosion would eventually win, especially after seeing it had already done so on the far eastern side of the Shattered Plains, but that was probably eons away.

script.text: The other two dove after him, exposing their backs to Sigzil—who dove as well, summoning Vienta as a long Shardlance. He rammed it through one of their backs, then formed a Blade to sweep at the other—all while they fell together.

If the Lightweavers did their job right, Deepest Ones—who peeked through walls and scouted the area—would soon give the report that a huge gemstone stash was there, heavily guarded. Hopefully not suspiciously so.

script.text: It was a perfect feint. Just subtle enough, just tempting enough. He had to hope it worked, because those Focused Ones were breaking the wall of Narak Prime—and the Stonewards were running low on Light to repair it.

Deepest Ones emerged from stone where the wooden protections had been broken, while Magnified Ones with hulking silhouettes clashed against Stonewards who liquefied the ground.

script.text: It was madness. Traditional battle lines and formations were almost impossible to maintain. script.text: in the darkness, his crystalline eyes and crown glowing with their own light. Contrasting with the boiling red ocean of clouds above. Then Moash shot into the air and whipped a knife from his belt, slashing with it as something flew overhead.
script.speaker: Narrator

script.text: Sigzil felt Vienta’s pain as his own, though the anti-Stormlight knife had barely nicked her. She became visible, dropping, a small figure in a puff of blue cloth who struck the ground near him, her arm completely destroyed and leaking Stormlight, her eyes wide as she trembled and gasped.
script.speaker: Narrator

script.text: Moash landed again, fabrial in one hand, light-bending knife in the other.

script.speaker: Unknown

script.text: he said.

script.speaker: Narrator

script.text: A flash of light sent them through the Oathgate, and as soon as they appeared on the other side, he heard the orders to lock the mechanism so no enemies could follow. That would work, but would isolate and cut off the Shattered Plains.
script.speaker: Narrator

script.text: An Edgedancer came skating up to heal him. Though his body began working again, Sigzil lay in a heap on the ground, staring at the Shardblade they placed beside him.
script.speaker: Narrator

script.text: Relief never came. Painspren crawled all over him. For no amount of Radiant healing could fix the pain that he felt deep within.
script.speaker: Narrator

script.text: As Thundercloud munched corpses, Venli leaned against him, trembling, understanding from the wild ride how the top of a drum might feel after an extended solo. The other listeners seemed equally unnerved—all but Thude, who was
script.speaker: Narrator

script.text: Venli hummed to Resolve, then went on wobbling feet to retrieve the package Sigzil had tossed for her. Just some papers rolled in an oiled cloth, which she tucked away for tomorrow. Narak was eerily empty now, barely
script.speaker: Narrator

script.text: recognizable. Wet, crumpled buildings. Pools of rainwater, and little rainspren peeking up among the debris.
script.speaker: Narrator

script.text: Fresh bodies left to make it appear like the assault had been more effective than it had actually been. She maintained Resolve, but secretly thought it looked obvious that the chasmfiends had attacked unpopulated sections. That the humans had evacuated willingly. That the retreat had been too quick.
script.speaker: Narrator

script.text: She held her breath as El himself was carried onto the plateau by a Heavenly One. And Venli realized she still had no idea what brand of Fused he was. What were
script.speaker: Narrator

script.text: powers? She’d heard that he did the replacement of his carapace himself, putting metal where there should be chitin, but any brand of Fused could heal from such wounds.
script.speaker: Narrator

script.text: He strolled through the camp, and eventually paused beside Venli and her crew. Leshwi and the others landed nearby. The Oathgate flashed again. Seconds later a Voidspren—like a line of glowing red light—crossed the ground.
script.speaker: Narrator

script.text: “That is the last of them,”
script.speaker: Unknown

script.text: a familiar voice said.
script.speaker: Narrator

script.text: “I watched them go. Vyre had some fun at the end, but it is done now. The Shattered Plains have fallen to us at last.”
script.speaker: Unknown

script.text: “Your group did well,”
script.speaker: Unknown

script.text: El said, looking to Venli.
script.speaker: Narrator

script.text: “Retreat with your people to the staging plateau. This might be a feint; the humans do like an unexpected rally. It is … something curious about them.”
script.speaker: Unknown

script.text: Venli nodded, but quietly sent a request to Thundercloud. He ambled toward them, a human arm hanging from his mouth, and flopped down right there and closed his eyes. The other two joined him, maws bloodied.
script.speaker: Narrator

script.text: “There’
script.speaker: Unknown

script.text: ll be no moving them now, Grand One,
script.speaker: Narrator

script.text: ” Thude said. “
script.speaker: Unknown

script.text: They are burst predators—a lot of activity and feasting, followed by a good nap.”
script.speaker: Narrator

script.text: “I suppose we can watch this plateau from here, Ancient One,”
script.speaker: Unknown

script.text: Venli said to the Fused.
script.speaker: Narrator

script.text: “Very well,”
script.speaker: Unknown

script.text: El said, and moved on, speaking with his Fused commanders and posting the majority of his forces near the Oathgate—he had Vyre, the traitor, lock it down from their side, but seemed worried the humans might somehow reverse that.
script.speaker: Narrator

script.text: He was watching for the wrong kind of trap. Venli and the others gathered in a huddle, and none dared hum the rhythms they were feeling. Except for Timbre, deep within her.
script.speaker: Narrator

script.text: Optimistic Joy. Had it … actually worked?
script.speaker: Narrator

script.text: They’d see on the morrow.
script.speaker: Narrator

script.text: It is often said that the best teacher is failure. This is true. But it is also the best killer. May you be lucky enough in failure to live, and unlucky enough in success to struggle.
script.speaker: Narrator

script.text: The surgeon put some ointment on the stump to dull the pain, and didn’t order bed rest. He kept glancing at the dome in the waning evening light. Another runner came with a message for Adolin, Kushkam asking for some
script.speaker: Narrator

script.speaker: Unknown

script.speaker: Unknown

script.text: Adolin drew in a deep breath, then nodded. So it was that a few minutes later, he found himself in another game of towers with Yanagawn. Using the familiarity of the game to try, for a short time at least, to get his mind off his worries. The emperor won their first bout. He had all the signs of becoming an excellent field general—just the right willingness to seize opportunities. Not timid, but also not brash. He learned from mistakes, and rarely had to be taught the same principle twice.
script.speaker: Narrator

script.text: Adolin settled back, rubbing his stump—as he’d removed the peg for the moment. He was coming to understand how lucky the Azish were. Out of the hundreds of boys who could have been plucked from the street, how had they—or really, Lift—found the one who would actually make a great leader?
script.speaker: Narrator

script.text: Unless … how many people who lived in the gutters would have excelled if put in this seat? After his conversation with Colot the night before, Adolin found himself questioning things he never had previously. Like what it meant to be the Blackthorn
script.speaker: Narrator

script.text: ’s son. He’
script.speaker: Unknown

script.text: d always assumed that the Almighty had put him in that role deliberately. But if the Almighty was dead …
script.speaker: Narrator

script.text: They reset the pieces. Tense, as another report came in. This was the last stand. All defenders on the lines, all reserves called up and fighting, no one being allowed to rest for more than fifteen-minute bursts. The next few hours would determine the fate of Azir for centuries to come. But here, two of the most powerful men in the world could do nothing but sit and wait.
script.speaker: Narrator

script.text: So they played. Adolin
script.speaker: Narrator

script.speaker: Unknown

She eyed the game board in her analytical way. Then she nodded. He knew she played with her father—indeed, they

script.text: “Adolin, your aunt has returned, but not your father. Brightness Navani can’
script.speaker: Unknown

script.speaker: Narrator

script.text: ’d spent too long hoping for the Azish reinforcements. He glanced up as he heard distant horns, but it wasn’

script.text: t a call for the wounded yet. Only a warning that no shift change was coming. No one would sleep tonight. Unfortunately, exhausted soldiers were better than no soldiers.
script.speaker: Narrator

script.text: Yanagawn placed his next piece, and in so doing took a dominant position on the game board. He sat back, pleased—and rightly so. He was doing better than either Adolin or May. Therefore it was satisfying to watch Yanagawn’s complete disbelief as, over the next half hour, he was systematically destroyed.
script.speaker: Narrator

script.text: Yanagawn scrambled to recover. He tried to employ the tactics Adolin had taught him. He made a few mistakes, a great number of ordinary moves, and even a few legitimately brilliant ones. He lost anyway, crushed as May and Adolin allied against him. Adolin quickly mopped up May, who was forced to retreat—though she finished with more points than Yanagawn. Which had likely been one of her best outcomes. He could tell she was proud of doing as well as she had; towers was rarely taught to women. Indeed, he’d heard that women had trouble finding capable opponents willing to play them.
script.speaker: Narrator

script.text: “How?”
script.speaker: Unknown

script.text: Yanagawn said, looking at the dismal results.
script.speaker: Narrator

script.text: “How did I lose? You two talked it through ahead of time and decided to defeat me together?”
script.speaker: Unknown

script.text: “No,”
script.speaker: Unknown

script.text: May said.
script.speaker: Narrator

script.text: “We simply played by best principles.”
script.speaker: Unknown

script.text: Adolin leaned forward.
script.speaker: Narrator

script.text: “This is a lesson that doesn’
script.speaker: Unknown

script.text: t come up very often in real life, but it’s
script.speaker: Narrator

script.text: to learn, because when it
script.speaker: Narrator

script.text: come up it can lead to disaster. You remember my key lesson? The most powerful force wins?”
script.speaker: Narrator

script.text: “Unless,”
script.speaker: Unknown

script.text: Yanagawn said,
script.speaker: Narrator

script.text: “terrain, incompetence, or random chance interfere.”
script.speaker: Unknown

script.text: the most powerful force!”
script.speaker: Narrator

script.text: “No,”
script.speaker: Unknown

script.text: Adolin said, and gestured at the board. “May and I
script.speaker: Narrator

script.text: were. This is the lesson, Yanagawn. In a contest of one-on-one, you should present power and dominate every chance you get. However, in a contest between three or
script.speaker: Narrator

script.text: parties, that
script.speaker: Narrator

script.text: ’s not the case.”
script.speaker: Unknown

script.text: “Two weaker forces,”
script.speaker: Unknown

script.text: May said,
script.speaker: Narrator

script.text: “will always align against the strongest one. By presenting strength, you become a target, galvanizing your enemies to put aside their differences.”
script.speaker: Unknown

script.text: She began cleaning up the pieces, admiring the detailed silvery figurines.
script.speaker: Narrator

script.text: “My father talked about this a great deal during the days of the squabbling highprinces. It can get messy when there are ten participants all choosing sides …”
script.speaker: Unknown

script.text: “It’
script.speaker: Unknown

script.text: s sometimes called the Sunmaker
script.speaker: Narrator

script.text: ’s Gambit,”
script.speaker: Unknown

script.text: Adolin added.
script.speaker: Narrator

script.speaker: Unknown

script.text: Yanagawn stared at the board.
script.speaker: Narrator

script.text: “So … what should I have done?”
script.speaker: Unknown

script.text: “Play more carefully,”
script.speaker: Unknown

script.text: Adolin said.
script.speaker: Narrator

script.text: “Feign weakness. Or make alliances early.”
script.speaker: Unknown

script.text: He paused, then shrugged. “Or build up enough power that you alone are stronger than
script.speaker: Narrator

script.text: of your opponents at once. That
script.speaker: Narrator

script.text: ’s hard, but valid too.”
script.speaker: Unknown

script.text: “That sounds complicated,”
script.speaker: Unknown

script.text: Yanagawn said.
script.speaker: Narrator

script.text: “Welcome to politics,”
script.speaker: Unknown

script.text: Adolin said. “Two parties on a battlefield is merely warfare: they fight until one leaves. Three parties on a battlefield is a negotiation; it transforms into an
script.speaker: Narrator

script.text: different game.
script.speaker: Narrator

script.text: ” He shook his head. “

script.text: “One I’
script.speaker: Unknown

script.text: m bad at. Sword on sword is so much cleaner.

script.text: ” Adolin looked up at Yanagawn. “

script.text: But listen, this game tries to replicate the real battlefield—and in this case it does. Multiple players makes things messy. Learn the lesson.”

script.text: Yanagawn gave him a frown, but Adolin finished tidying the pieces. He’d always hated the fourth rule. It seemed to favor people like his father. It—
script.speaker: Narrator

script.text: The horns sounded once more.
script.speaker: Narrator

script.text: That was it. A desperate signal, the type Kushkam had sent warnings he might need. All able-bodied men were called, regardless of experience. The city was appallingly short on men at this point; too many had been recruited for the battles to the south, and too many others had fled the city or been sent to farming operations to feed the armies.
script.speaker: Narrator

script.text: Anyone left was called to come—including the crippled, the elderly, and any women willing to fight. That would include Adolin, who started strapping on his peg. He wouldn’t wear the Plate, but he could hold a shield and
script.speaker: Narrator

script.text: keep his balance. He quested out to Maya, to check if maybe he could get a Blade.
script.speaker: Narrator

script.text: Hours. Some hours. Difficult to judge in the beads.
